tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The soup was hot enough to warm us after the hike.
The soup was enough hot to warm us after the hike.
It was such a noisy café that we could barely talk.
It was so a noisy café that we could barely talk.
The trail was too steep for beginners.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The soup was hot enough to warm us after the hike.**

Hot enough places enough after the adjective, which is the standard slot before a to-infinitive. The soup was hot enough to warm us reads as natural, living English and matches the sufficiency pattern you want after a hike.
**B) The soup was enough hot to warm us after the hike.**

Enough cannot sit before the adjective here. Flip to hot enough (or switch the meaning to too hot if you mean excess).
**C) It was such a noisy café that we could barely talk.**

Such a + adjective + singular countable noun + that-clause is the classic result pattern. Such a noisy café that… correctly intensifies the whole noun phrase, not just the adjective alone.
**D) It was so a noisy café that we could barely talk.**

So does not combine with a before a noun. Repair to such a noisy café that…, or drop the noun and write so noisy that…
**E) The trail was too steep for beginners.**

Too + adjective (+ for…) correctly marks excess relative to a purpose or audience. Too steep for beginners is exactly the shape you want when the trail goes past what beginners can handle.
tasks.solution_overview:
These five lines swap so, such, too, and enough around everyday food, cafés, and hiking talk. You are deciding whether each sentence is grammatical as written—not whether you like the word choice.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

The focus is partnering each intensifier with the right kind of word, and keeping enough after adjectives. So wants an adjective or adverb; such wants a noun phrase; too marks excess before an adjective; enough after an adjective signals "sufficient for a purpose." Easy misspellings of the pattern are really word-order errors: so a… and enough + adjective.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

For each letter, spot the intensifier first, then check what sits immediately after it. If the partner type or order is wrong, mark false; if the classic pattern holds (adj + enough, such a + noun, too + adj), mark true.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The fog was so thick that the ferry stayed in harbour.
There was such excitement that the crowd started cheering early.
There was so excitement that the crowd started cheering early.
He is not tall enough for the roller coaster.
He is not enough tall for the roller coaster.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The fog was so thick that the ferry stayed in harbour.**

So + adjective + that-clause intensifies the quality and links a clear result. So thick that the ferry stayed in harbour keeps the adjective alone in so's slot and lets that introduce what followed.
**B) There was such excitement that the crowd started cheering early.**

Such + uncountable noun (excitement) + that needs no article. There was such excitement that… correctly treats excitement as a mass noun under such.
**C) There was so excitement that the crowd started cheering early.**

So cannot modify a bare noun. Repair to such excitement or so much excitement that…
**D) He is not tall enough for the roller coaster.**

Tall enough places enough after the adjective and before for. He is not tall enough for the roller coaster is the everyday sufficiency pattern under negation.
**E) He is not enough tall for the roller coaster.**

Enough tall reverses the required order. Flip to tall enough; only when a noun follows (enough time) can enough come first.
tasks.solution_overview:
Fog, ferry delays, crowd noise, and a roller-coaster height check — each sentence turns on so, such, or enough. Judge only the grammar of the intensifier pattern, not how dramatic the scene sounds.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Pair each intensifier with its partner: so with adjectives (and result that-clauses), such with nouns, and enough after adjectives before for / to…. When so sits bare before a noun with no much/many, the structure collapses.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Scan left to right for so / such / enough, then ask what word class follows. Correct partners stay true; so + bare noun or enough + adjective flips to false.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 3
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: It was such an early train that half the carriages were empty.
It was so an early train that half the carriages were empty.
The suitcase is too heavy to lift alone.
The lecture was too much technical for first-year students.
She sang so beautifully that the hall went silent.
tactical_explanations:
**A) It was such an early train that half the carriages were empty.**

Such an before a vowel-sound adjective + noun is correct — early begins with a vowel sound, so an is right. Such an early train that… builds the full noun phrase under such and adds a result clause.
**B) It was so an early train that half the carriages were empty.**

So an is ungrammatical. Replace with such an early train that…, or restructure as so early that… without parking the noun after so.
**C) The suitcase is too heavy to lift alone.**

Too + adjective + to-infinitive expresses excess that blocks a result. The suitcase is too heavy to lift alone means the weight stops a solo lift — a clean too…to pattern.
**D) The lecture was too much technical for first-year students.**

Do not insert much between too and a single adjective. Write too technical; reserve too much for nouns (too much noise).
**E) She sang so beautifully that the hall went silent.**

So + adverb + that-clause parallels so + adjective. She sang so beautifully that the hall went silent intensifies manner and states the result without dragging a noun into so's slot.
tasks.solution_overview:
Early trains, heavy suitcases, technical lectures, and a quiet hall after a song — the sentences lean on such, so, and too. Your job is to accept clean patterns and reject article or much mistakes.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Watch article choice with such (such an before a vowel sound) and the too much trap before a lone adjective. So an… is never a substitute for such an…, and so + adverb + that is fine when you intensify manner.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

If you see so / such before an article + noun, ask whether such owns that noun phrase. If too is followed by much + adjective (not a noun), mark false; keep too + adj + to and so + adverb + that as true.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 4
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: We had enough daylight to finish photographing the mural.
The path was so icy that cyclists walked their bikes.
She typed so quickly notes that nobody could read them.
The film was such gripping that we stayed until the credits.
The kitchen is large enough for a second fridge.
tactical_explanations:
**A) We had enough daylight to finish photographing the mural.**

Enough + noun is correct when enough quantifies a noun. We had enough daylight to finish photographing the mural treats daylight as the thing of which there was a sufficient amount.
**B) The path was so icy that cyclists walked their bikes.**

So + adjective + that correctly builds cause and result. The path was so icy that cyclists walked their bikes keeps icy in the adjective slot after so.
**C) She typed so quickly notes that nobody could read them.**

So quickly notes mixes the adverb pattern with a noun sitting where that or an infinitive should be. Repair to so quickly that… or such quick notes that…
**D) The film was such gripping that we stayed until the credits.**

Such needs a noun phrase: such a gripping film that…, not such gripping alone before that. Without a noun head, such has nothing to intensify.
**E) The kitchen is large enough for a second fridge.**

Adjective + enough + for + noun phrase is grammatical. The kitchen is large enough for a second fridge places enough after large and licenses the for-complement.
tasks.solution_overview:
Daylight for photography, icy paths, typing speed, a gripping film, and kitchen space — again so / such / enough decide truth. Separate quantity enough from adjective enough before you judge hybrids.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Enough + noun quantifies (enough daylight); adjective + enough describes sufficiency of a quality. Hybrid errors stack words from different patterns: so + adverb + noun, or such + bare adjective with no noun head.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Ask whether enough is quantifying a noun or finishing an adjective. Then check that so's next word is adj/adv only, and that such still has a noun phrase before that.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 5
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: There was so much rain that the cricket match was abandoned.
There were so many volunteers that the charity ran out of badges.
The recipe is too vaguely to follow without a video.
The offer was not generous enough to tempt her back.
It was such bad weather that the outdoor market closed early.
tactical_explanations:
**A) There was so much rain that the cricket match was abandoned.**

So much + uncountable noun (+ that) is the correct so + noun pattern. There was so much rain that the cricket match was abandoned pairs much with uncountable rain and states the result.
**B) There were so many volunteers that the charity ran out of badges.**

So many + plural countable noun is parallel to so much. There were so many volunteers that… correctly chooses many for a plural count noun.
**C) The recipe is too vaguely to follow without a video.**

Too must modify an adjective after be when you mean the recipe itself: too vague to follow, not too vaguely. The -ly form is wrong for a subject complement here.
**D) The offer was not generous enough to tempt her back.**

Generous enough to… places enough correctly after the adjective. The offer was not generous enough to tempt her back is the standard not + adj + enough to… exam shape.
**E) It was such bad weather that the outdoor market closed early.**

Such + adjective + uncountable noun (weather) needs no article. It was such bad weather that the outdoor market closed early is textbook such + mass noun phrasing.
tasks.solution_overview:
Rain, volunteers, a vague recipe, a job offer, and bad weather — quantity so much/many and such with uncountables sit beside a too + adverb slip. Count the noun before you choose much or many.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

When so modifies quantity, check much (uncountable) versus many (plural countable). When too follows be, prefer an adjective describing the subject. Such before an uncountable noun phrase usually drops the article.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Identify whether the intensifier is grading quantity, quality, or excess. So much / so many + matching noun stays true; too + -ly after be when you mean the thing itself is false; adj + enough and such + adj + uncountable noun stay true.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 6
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The app loads too slowly to be useful during live quizzes.
The photos were such blurry that we deleted the whole roll.
We do not have enough flour to bake a second loaf.
It was so narrow a bridge that only one car could cross.
The library was enough quiet for evening revision.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The app loads too slowly to be useful during live quizzes.**

Too + adverb + to-infinitive correctly marks excess manner blocking a purpose. The app loads too slowly to be useful during live quizzes parallels too small to… with an adverb instead of an adjective.
**B) The photos were such blurry that we deleted the whole roll.**

Such blurry lacks a noun head. Use such blurry photos that… or so blurry that…
**C) We do not have enough flour to bake a second loaf.**

Enough + uncountable noun (flour) is correct before to. We do not have enough flour to bake a second loaf quantifies the ingredient, not an adjective.
**D) It was so narrow a bridge that only one car could cross.**

So + adjective + a + noun (+ that) is a formal but grammatical pattern. It was so narrow a bridge that only one car could cross matches such a narrow bridge in meaning while keeping the article after the adjective.
**E) The library was enough quiet for evening revision.**

Quiet is an adjective, so use quiet enough, not enough quiet. Flip enough to the post-adjective slot for evening revision.
tasks.solution_overview:
Slow apps, blurry photos, baking flour, a narrow bridge, and a quiet library — patterns range from everyday too…to… to the formal so + adj + a + noun. Do not mark a rarer formal pattern false just because such a… is more common.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Watch for such + bare adjective (needs a noun) and enough + adjective (must flip). Too + adverb + to is fine when manner is excessive, and enough + uncountable noun is the quantity slot.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Check each intensifier's partner word class. Accept so narrow a bridge as a formal twin of such a narrow bridge; fail enough quiet and such blurry that…

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 7
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The deadline is tight enough that any delay will cost us the slot.
It was so clever puzzle that the whole class stayed late.
The courier arrived too late for us to catch the evening train.
Such were the crowds that the museum opened an extra wing.
The essay is too much short for a full literature review.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The deadline is tight enough that any delay will cost us the slot.**

Adjective + enough + that-clause is acceptable alongside enough to…. The deadline is tight enough that any delay will cost us the slot still means "sufficiently tight," with that spelling out the consequence.
**B) It was so clever puzzle that the whole class stayed late.**

So clever puzzle misses the article/noun patterning needed with a countable singular. Use such a clever puzzle that… or so clever that…
**C) The courier arrived too late for us to catch the evening train.**

Too + adverb/adjective + for + object + to-infinitive is a solid excess pattern. The courier arrived too late for us to catch the evening train means we could not catch it in time.
**D) Such were the crowds that the museum opened an extra wing.**

Inversion such were the crowds that… is formal but grammatical. Such + be + noun phrase + that intensifies the noun phrase with literary word order — still correct on a true/false grammar check.
**E) The essay is too much short for a full literature review.**

Too much short wrongly inserts much before an adjective. Use too short; save too much for nouns.
tasks.solution_overview:
Deadlines, puzzles, late couriers, museum crowds, and short essays — most items still hinge on so/such/too word order, but one formal inversion with such is legitimately correct. Unusual word order is not automatically wrong.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Keep policing partners of so and the too much + adjective error. Adj + enough + that is acceptable, and such were the crowds that… is literary inversion, not a slip. So + adj + countable noun without a remains a classic miss.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Accept tight enough that… and the inverted such were…. Fail so clever puzzle (missing article patterning) and too much short (much before an adjective).

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 8
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The map was not clear enough for hikers to follow in mist.
They made so rapid progress that the language course finished early.
They made such rapid progress that the language course finished early.
The backpack is too heavily to carry up the ridge.
We kept enough spare batteries to last the whole festival.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The map was not clear enough for hikers to follow in mist.**

Not + adjective + enough + for + noun + to-infinitive is fully grammatical. The map was not clear enough for hikers to follow in mist licenses the for…to… complement after enough.
**B) They made so rapid progress that the language course finished early.**

So + adjective + uncountable noun (progress) without a is acceptable because progress is uncountable. They made so rapid progress that… contrasts with countable so clever puzzle, which needs an article.
**C) They made such rapid progress that the language course finished early.**

Such + adjective + uncountable noun is the safer textbook twin of the previous pattern. They made such rapid progress that… is the exam-safe default many teachers prefer.
**D) The backpack is too heavily to carry up the ridge.**

Too heavily is an adverb where an adjective is needed after be. Write too heavy to carry… (or restructure with a different verb if you truly need an adverb).
**E) We kept enough spare batteries to last the whole festival.**

Enough + adjective + plural noun quantifies how many of that type you have. We kept enough spare batteries to last the whole festival means a sufficient number of that kind — noun phrase after enough, not the illegal enough + bare adjective flip.
tasks.solution_overview:
Misty hiking maps, language progress, overloaded backpacks, and spare batteries — countable versus uncountable after so/such matters, and be still wants an adjective after too. Enough before a noun phrase is not the enough + adjective error.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Distinguish countable vs uncountable after so/such, and adjective vs adverb after linking be. So + adj + uncountable noun (so rapid progress) can work; such rapid progress is the safer twin. Too heavily after be is the wrong word class.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

If the noun is uncountable, both so adj + noun and such adj + noun may be true. Fail adverbials after be where an adjective describes the subject; accept not + adj + enough for…to… and enough + noun phrase.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 9
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The view was so stunning as to stop us mid-sentence.
The view was such stunning as to stop us mid-sentence.
The oven is not hot enough to crisp the pastry.
It was too a complicated route for a first visit.
There has been such an upsurge in tickets that the box office stayed open late.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The view was so stunning as to stop us mid-sentence.**

So + adjective + as to + infinitive is a formal result pattern parallel to so…that. The view was so stunning as to stop us mid-sentence means the view was stunning enough that it stopped us.
**B) The view was such stunning as to stop us mid-sentence.**

** Such pairs with nouns; so…as to pairs with adjectives.

Trap: Such does not take as to after a bare adjective. Use so stunning as to… or such a stunning view that…
**C) The oven is not hot enough to crisp the pastry.**

Not + adjective + enough + to… is correct. The oven is not hot enough to crisp the pastry places enough after hot before the purpose infinitive.
**D) It was too a complicated route for a first visit.**

** Too + adj + a + noun is possible (too complicated a route), but too a… never is.

Trap: Too a complicated wrongly puts the article right after too. Use too complicated a route or such a complicated route — never too a…
**E) There has been such an upsurge in tickets that the box office stayed open late.**

Such an + noun (+ that) correctly intensifies a countable singular. There has been such an upsurge in tickets that… chooses an because upsurge is countable singular.
tasks.solution_overview:
Stunning views, pastry, complicated routes, and ticket surges — formal so…as to… enters alongside ordinary enough and such. Treat the elevated pattern as fair game when the pieces fit.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

So + adjective + as to + infinitive parallels so…that for result. Such does not take as to after a bare adjective, and too never precedes the article directly (too a…). Such an + countable singular remains standard.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Accept so stunning as to… and hot enough / such an upsurge. Fail such stunning as to… and too a complicated…; remember the repair too complicated a route is possible, but too a… never is.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 10
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The novel is too dense a book for a single weekend.
Fans left because the queue was such long.
We arrived early enough to claim seats near the stage.
The coach found the warm-up so rushed that she ordered another lap.
She is enough experienced to lead the climbing group.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The novel is too dense a book for a single weekend.**

Too + adjective + a + noun (+ for…) is a formal pattern matching so adj a noun. The novel is too dense a book for a single weekend means an excessively dense book for that timeframe.
**B) Fans left because the queue was such long.**

** Bare such + adjective without noun is incomplete.

Trap: Such long needs a noun: such a long queue, or else so long that…. Bare such + adjective without a noun is incomplete.
**C) We arrived early enough to claim seats near the stage.**

Adverb early + enough + to-infinitive is correct — enough follows the adverb just as it follows adjectives. We arrived early enough to claim seats near the stage is everyday event English.
**D) The coach found the warm-up so rushed that she ordered another lap.**

So + adjective + that after a reporting verb is clean. The coach found the warm-up so rushed that she ordered another lap keeps so on the adjective in the object complement.
**E) She is enough experienced to lead the climbing group.**

** Same flip rule as enough hot.

Trap: Experienced is an adjective, so write experienced enough, not enough experienced. Same flip rule as enough hot.
tasks.solution_overview:
Dense novels, long queues, early arrivals, rushed warm-ups, and climbing experience — formal too/so + adj + a + noun shapes appear beside the usual enough and such traps. Article placement after the adjective is the tell.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Accept too/so + adjective + a + noun when the article lands after the adjective. Reject such + bare adjective and enough + adjective, which recycle the same order mistakes from easier tasks.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

If you see too/so + adj + a + noun + for/that, treat it as formal but true. Fail such long without a noun, and flip enough experienced to experienced enough.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 11
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The storm was so fierce as that ferries cancelled sailings.
The storm was so fierce that ferries cancelled sailings.
We lacked enough evidence to challenge the referee's call.
It was such a poorly printed map that hikers took wrong turns.
The hills are too steep for the juniors finish before dusk.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The storm was so fierce as that ferries cancelled sailings.**

** Never stack as and that after so.

Trap: So…as that mixes two patterns. Choose so…that or so…as to, not both markers stacked.
**B) The storm was so fierce that ferries cancelled sailings.**

Clean so + adjective + that result clause. The storm was so fierce that ferries cancelled sailings uses one linker only.
**C) We lacked enough evidence to challenge the referee's call.**

Enough + noun (evidence) before a to-infinitive is correct. We lacked enough evidence to challenge the referee's call quantifies an uncountable noun under enough.
**D) It was such a poorly printed map that hikers took wrong turns.**

Such a + adverb + adjective + noun is fine when the adverb modifies the adjective inside the noun phrase. It was such a poorly printed map that hikers took wrong turns — the whole noun phrase still sits after such.
**E) The hills are too steep for the juniors finish before dusk.**

** For + object needs to before the verb.

Trap: Missing to before the infinitive: write too steep for the juniors to finish before dusk. For + object needs to before the verb.
tasks.solution_overview:
Fierce storms, referee disputes, poorly printed maps, and steep hills for juniors — blended result markers and a missing to after for + object are the hard catches. Such can still head a heavily modified noun phrase.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Hunt stacked linkers after so (as that mixes two patterns) and missing to in too…for X [to] V. Enough + noun before to remains the quantity pattern; such a + adverb + adjective + noun is fine when everything modifies the noun head.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Choose exactly one result linker after so: that or as to, never as that. Keep enough evidence and such a poorly printed map; add to before finish in the juniors line.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 12
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Practice stopped because the heat became so intense.
Practice stopped because the heat became such intense.
The clause is worded carefully enough to avoid confusion.
There were too few lifeguards to watch every lane.
The gallery hung so few paintings that the room felt empty.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Practice stopped because the heat became so intense.**

So + adjective can stand without a that-clause when the result is implied by context. Practice stopped because the heat became so intense — that-clause is common but not obligatory.
**B) Practice stopped because the heat became such intense.**

** After become, prefer so + adjective.

Trap: Such intense needs a noun (such intense heat) or a switch to so intense. After become, prefer so + adjective for a subject complement.
**C) The clause is worded carefully enough to avoid confusion.**

Carefully enough places enough after the adverb modifying how the clause is worded. The clause is worded carefully enough to avoid confusion works like adj + enough + to…
**D) There were too few lifeguards to watch every lane.**

Too few + plural noun expresses insufficiency — an excess of scarcity. There were too few lifeguards to watch every lane is grammatical and means roughly not enough lifeguards.
**E) The gallery hung so few paintings that the room felt empty.**

So few + plural noun + that is grammatical and parallel to so many. The gallery hung so few paintings that the room felt empty pairs few with a plural count noun under so.
tasks.solution_overview:
Intense heat stopping practice, careful wording, short staffing of lifeguards, and a sparse gallery wall — result that-clauses are optional here. The real test is whether such has a noun and whether few sits correctly after so/too.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

So + adjective can stand alone when context implies the result. Such still needs a noun head after become. Too few / so few + plural noun are grammatical quantity patterns, not the too much + adjective error.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

If such + adjective has no noun, mark false. Accept bare so intense, carefully enough to…, too few lifeguards, and so few paintings that…

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 13
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The rule is such that latecomers wait for the next tour.
The rule is so that latecomers wait for the next tour.
Runners pulled out, the course having become too muddy to race.
She left enough of a gap to let the next cyclist pass.
The trail is not enough marked for night walking.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The rule is such that latecomers wait for the next tour.**

Such that meaning "of a kind that" is a fixed formal pattern without an adjective after such. The rule is such that latecomers wait for the next tour means the nature of the rule produces that outcome.
**B) The rule is so that latecomers wait for the next tour.**

** So that ≠ such that; different jobs.

Trap: So that expresses purpose ("in order that"), not the "of a kind that" reading. Here such that is required if you mean the rule's character.
**C) Runners pulled out, the course having become too muddy to race.**

Too + adjective + to-infinitive inside a participial absolute is still grammatical. Runners pulled out, the course having become too muddy to race keeps the too…to shape in a reduced clause.
**D) She left enough of a gap to let the next cyclist pass.**

Enough of a + singular countable noun is idiomatic. She left enough of a gap to let the next cyclist pass — of a(n) before the singular count noun is the natural frame.
**E) The trail is not enough marked for night walking.**

** Flip enough after adjectives even with not.

Trap: Marked is adjectival here, so write not marked enough, not not enough marked. Flip enough after the adjective even under negation.
tasks.solution_overview:
Tour rules, muddy race courses, bike gaps, and marked trails — harder items separate such that (nature/result) from so that (purpose), and test enough of a… plus adjective–enough order under negation.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Such that meaning "of a kind that" is a fixed formal pattern. So that marks purpose ("in order that") and cannot swap in for that reading. Enough of a + singular countable noun is idiomatic; enough still follows adjectives even with not.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Ask whether the clause describes the nature of the rule (such that) or a purpose (so that). Accept too…to inside reduced clauses and enough of a gap; flip not enough marked to not marked enough.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 14
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Attendance fell so low as volunteers began cancelling shifts.
Attendance fell so low that volunteers began cancelling shifts.
The visa proved too costly a requirement for the exchange student.
We cannot cook without such spices as the recipe lists.
The rebuild was enough extensive that the gallery closed for a year.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Attendance fell so low as volunteers began cancelling shifts.**

** So adj as + finite clause is not standard for result.

Trap: So…as without to needs a different reading; here a result clause should use that (or so low as to cause…). So adj as + finite clause is not standard for result.
**B) Attendance fell so low that volunteers began cancelling shifts.**

So + adjective + that correctly states the result. Attendance fell so low that volunteers began cancelling shifts is the default result pattern.
**C) The visa proved too costly a requirement for the exchange student.**

Too + adjective + a + noun (+ for…) is grammatical formal English. The visa proved too costly a requirement for the exchange student ≈ an excessively costly requirement.
**D) We cannot cook without such spices as the recipe lists.**

Such…as meaning "the kind that" with a relative-like clause is correct. We cannot cook without such spices as the recipe lists = the spices that the recipe lists.
**E) The rebuild was enough extensive that the gallery closed for a year.**

** Enough never precedes the adjective in this frame.

Trap: Enough extensive reverses order; need extensive enough that…. Enough never precedes the adjective in this frame.
tasks.solution_overview:
Falling attendance, costly visas, listed spices, and a long rebuild — result linkers after so, formal too adj a noun, and such…as all appear. Enough + adjective is still illegal.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Separate result that from faulty so…as + finite clause. Formal such…as ("the kind that") and too + adjective + a + noun are acceptable. Keep policing enough before adjectives.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Default result linker after so is that (or as to + infinitive). Accept too costly a requirement and such spices as…; fail so low as volunteers… and enough extensive…

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 15
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The playlist was so arranged as to build toward the finale.

There was too little time remaining to rehearse the second act.
The dish became such favourite with locals that tourists queued daily.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The playlist was so arranged as to build toward the finale.**

So + past participle/adjective + as to + infinitive expresses designed result. The playlist was so arranged as to build toward the finale = arranged in such a way that it built toward the finale.
**B) Cash on hand is barely enough for bus fare, let alone a taxi.**

Enough for + noun works; barely intensifies sufficiency without breaking grammar. Cash on hand is barely enough for bus fare, let alone a taxi keeps enough in its quantity/sufficiency role.

**Tip:** ** Modifiers like barely/almost can precede enough.
**C) It was too little time remaining to rehearse the second act.**

** Watch dummy it with quantity noun phrases.

Trap: It was too little time is awkward/wrong for this quantity reading. Prefer there was / we had too little time, or too little time remained.
**D) There was too little time remaining to rehearse the second act.**

There was too little + uncountable noun (+ to…) is the natural existential pattern. There was too little time remaining to rehearse the second act frames the shortage cleanly.

**Tip:** ** Prefer there-insertion with too little/much + noun.
**E) The dish became such favourite with locals that tourists queued daily.**

** Countable singular after such almost always needs a/an.

Trap: Needs an article: such a favourite with… (or so popular with…). Countable singular after such almost always needs a/an.

Playlists, bus fare, rehearsal time, and a local favourite dish — existential framing with too little + noun and articles after such decide several letters. Surface similarity can hide a missing there or a/an.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Judge there was / we had with too little + noun, article requirements after such with countable singulars, and formal so…as to…. Barely can intensify enough without breaking the pattern.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Prefer there-insertion with too little/much + noun; fail dummy it was too little time…. Accept so arranged as to… and barely enough for…; add a before favourite.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 16
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The experiment is designed such that temperature stays constant.

**A) The experiment is designed such that temperature stays constant.**

Designed such that… means "in such a way that" and is standard in scientific English. The experiment is designed such that temperature stays constant is a normal lab-register pattern.

**Tip:** ** Verb + such that ≈ configured so that.
**B) The experiment is designed so that temperature stays constant.**

Designed so that… expressing purpose/result is also grammatical. Here so that and such that can both work, with so that leaning slightly more toward intended purpose.
**C) The dough proved elastic enough that it stretched without tearing.**

Adjective + enough + that-clause is acceptable. The dough proved elastic enough that it stretched without tearing = sufficiently elastic that it stretched without tearing.
**D) He spoke with so a confident tone that doubts faded.**

** So a… returns as a trap even in longer NPs.

Trap: So a confident tone is wrong; use such a confident tone or so confidently that…. So a… returns as a trap even inside longer noun phrases.
**E) We kept the talk short enough not to overrun the lunch break.**

Adjective + enough + not to-infinitive correctly encodes avoidance. We kept the talk short enough not to overrun the lunch break = sufficiently short to avoid overrunning.
tasks.solution_overview:
Lab temperature control, elastic dough, confident speaking, and a short talk — after verbs of designing, both so that and such that can be right. The old so a… trap still fails.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Designed such that… ("in such a way that") and designed so that… (purpose/result) are both grammatical with slightly different nuance. Adj + enough + that and enough not to… are valid; so a… is not.

Allow both designing linkers when the sentence is well formed. Fail so a confident tone; accept elastic enough that… and short enough not to…

tasks.title: Task 17
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Seldom is a coastline so eroded that no beach remains.
The tent proved insufficiently sturdy enough to survive the gale.
Her complaint was not so much unfair as poorly timed.
The delay was such that, had we waited, the concert would have started.
They priced the tickets too steeply for students to attend weekly.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Seldom is a coastline so eroded that no beach remains.**

Inversion with seldom does not break the inner so…that pattern. Seldom is a coastline so eroded that no beach remains — evaluate the so…that core as true.

**Tip:** ** Judge the so/such/too/enough core even inside inversion shells.
**B) The tent proved insufficiently sturdy enough to survive the gale.**

** One sufficiency tool per adjective phrase.

Trap: Insufficiently sturdy enough doubles the sufficiency marker. Use insufficiently sturdy or not sturdy enough — not both in one adjective phrase.
**C) Her complaint was not so much unfair as poorly timed.**

Not so much X as Y is an established correlative; so is required in this idiom. Her complaint was not so much unfair as poorly timed is grammatical even though this is not ordinary so + adjective intensification.
**D) The delay was such that, had we waited, the concert would have started.**

Such that introducing a counterfactual continuation is formal and correct. The delay was such that, had we waited, the concert would have started — such that can host complex follow-ons, including inverted conditionals.
**E) They priced the tickets too steeply for students to attend weekly.**

Too + adverb + for + noun + to-infinitive marks excess manner or cost. They priced the tickets too steeply for students to attend weekly parallels too steep for X to V, with the adverb modifying the verb priced.

**Tip:** ** Too steeply for X to V parallels too steep for X to V (adv vs adj depends on what is modified).
tasks.solution_overview:
Eroded coastlines, gale-hit tents, timed complaints, delayed concerts, and steep ticket prices — advanced packaging wraps familiar so/such/too cores in inversion and idioms. Reject double intensifiers; keep legitimate so idioms.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Inversion shells and correlative not so much…as… still hide a clean so/such/too/enough core you can judge. Insufficiently…enough doubles sufficiency marking. Too + adverb + for…to… remains available for excess manner or cost.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Judge the inner pattern even when seldom opens the sentence. Fail stacked insufficiently sturdy enough; accept not so much…as…, such that with a counterfactual continuation, and too steeply for students to…

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

So + adverb + as to + infinitive correctly states result after a comparative frame. No other runner moved so swiftly as to claim the lead overnight — so…as to… works with adverbs as well as adjectives.

**C) The rule is drawn tightly enough that substitutions need consent.**

Adverb/adjective + enough + that remains grammatical in careful register. The rule is drawn tightly enough that substitutions need consent = sufficiently tightly that…

tasks.solution_overview:
Overnight race leads, tightly drawn rules, thin daylight, and intuitive interfaces — stress-test so…as to… with adverbs and demand the right linker after so adj a noun. Degree modifiers before too are allowed.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

So + adverb + as to + infinitive works; such does not modify adverbs. Adv/adj + enough + that remains fine in careful register. Rather too… is idiomatic; so adj a noun needs that or as to, not bare as + finite clause.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Accept so swiftly as to…, tightly enough that…, and rather too little…. Fail such swiftly and so intuitive a design as users… (use that or as to need…).

tasks.title: Task 19
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Only then did the river become high enough for kayaking to look safe.
The study was based on so biased a sample that the conclusions collapsed.
The study was based on such biased a sample that the conclusions collapsed.
Supplies look healthy enough; still, they may prove too thin under strain.
He is too much of a perfectionist to submit an unfinished draft.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Only then did the river become high enough for kayaking to look safe.**

Inversion only then did… leaves high enough for… intact and grammatical. Only then did the river become high enough for kayaking to look safe — embedded enough patterns survive fronting and inversion.
**B) The study was based on so biased a sample that the conclusions collapsed.**

So + adjective + a + noun + that is the formal pattern even inside a prepositional phrase. The study was based on so biased a sample that the conclusions collapsed = such a biased sample in meaning.
**C) The study was based on such biased a sample that the conclusions collapsed.**

** Such a + adj + noun, never such adj a noun.

Trap: Such biased a sample mis-orders the article; need such a biased sample (article before the adjective). Never write such adj a noun.
**D) Supplies look healthy enough; still, they may prove too thin under strain.**

Two coordinated judgments: adjective + enough, and too + adjective, both well formed. Supplies look healthy enough; still, they may prove too thin under strain — enough and too can contrast without clashing.
**E) He is too much of a perfectionist to submit an unfinished draft.**

Too much of a + noun + to-infinitive is a fixed evaluative idiom. He is too much of a perfectionist to submit an unfinished draft = excessively perfectionist-like to submit it unfinished.
tasks.solution_overview:
Kayaking on a high river, biased samples, thin supplies, and perfectionists — article placement separates so adj a noun (correct) from such adj a noun (incorrect). The idiom too much of a… to… is also in play.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

So + adjective + a + noun keeps the article after the adjective; such wants such a + adjective + noun. Embedded enough patterns survive inversion. Enough and too can contrast in one sentence; too much of a + noun + to… is a fixed evaluative idiom.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Accept high enough inside only then did…, so biased a sample, healthy enough / too thin, and too much of a perfectionist to…. Fail such biased a sample (article must precede the adjective after such).

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 20

tactical_explanations:

Adjective + enough inside an inverted third conditional is grammatical. Had the ice been thick enough, the skaters would have crossed the lake — enough stays adjective-final even in had-conditionals.
**B) The rehearsal grew so protracted as nobody could finalise the cues.**

** As to + infinitive, or that + clause — not as + clause after so + adj.

Trap: So…as + finite clause is wrong for result; use so protracted that… or so protracted as to prevent…. Choose as to + infinitive, or that + clause — not as + clause after so + adj.
**C) Whatever the poster promises, service is seldom swift enough to match it.**

Seldom… enough to… correctly denies sufficiency. Whatever the poster promises, service is seldom swift enough to match it — frequency adverb + enough is fine.
**D) It remains too early a stage for full automation of bookings.**

Too + adjective + a + noun (+ for…) is formal but correct. It remains too early a stage for full automation of bookings = an excessively early stage.
**E) Their reply was so that we cancelled the booking at once.**

** Reply/situation + such that = character/result; so that = purpose.

Trap: So that marks purpose ("in order that"), not the nature/result reading needed here. Use such that we cancelled… or Their reply was so blunt that we cancelled…. Reply/situation + such that = character/result; so that = purpose.
tasks.solution_overview:
Icy lakes, long rehearsals, poster promises, early booking automation, and abrupt replies — the final set mixes conditionals, formal too adj a noun, and result-linker discipline after so. Keep such that versus so that distinct.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Enough keeps adjective-final order even in had-conditionals. Results after so want that or as to, not as + finite clause. Too + adjective + a + noun (+ for…) is formal but correct; reply/situation + so that wrongly reads as purpose when character/result is meant.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Accept thick enough in the inverted conditional, swift enough to…, and too early a stage…. Fail so protracted as nobody… and was so that we… (use such that or so + adj + that).

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE
